const r=await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > enrichment/bible/work/s087/discovery/prepared-20261005/87_18/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.24.4	Moses writes covenant words	The commentary names Moses as recipient of the first pages; after Sinai, Moses writes the LORD's words in a book, locating the written witness in Moses' own scriptural story.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.24.7	Book of the Covenant read aloud	The commentary links old pages to a recited teaching; here Moses reads the written covenant in the people's hearing, and they answer by undertaking to obey it.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.31.24	Moses completes the written Torah	The commentary says the current warning is already in ancient pages; this verse explicitly says Moses completed writing the words of the Torah in a book.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.26	Book kept as a witness	The commentary calls the first pages a witness against the charge of novelty; Moses orders the completed book placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel, giving the text a future-testimony role.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.11	Public reading of the Torah	The commentary connects scripture with a message heard rather than a page handed to the Prophet; Moses orders the Torah read aloud before all Israel at the appointed gathering.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.12	All Israel hears and learns	The commentary's pages preserve instruction for later hearers; this assembly includes men, women, children, and resident aliens so they hear, learn, and fear the LORD.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.13	Children learn through hearing	The commentary says the word reaches a later generation without the Prophet consulting a page; Moses specifically includes children who have not known the Torah, so they hear and learn it.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Neh.8.8	Reading with explanation	The commentary presents recitation as the means by which written teaching becomes present to hearers; in Nehemiah, Levites read from the Torah and explain its sense so the assembly understands.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.36.4	Jeremiah dictates a scroll	The commentary contrasts old written pages with the Prophet's received recitation; Jeremiah dictates the LORD's words and Baruch writes them on a scroll, making the prophet's speech a written document.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.36.10	Baruch reads the scroll publicly	The commentary joins ancient pages to audible proclamation; Baruch reads Jeremiah's scroll in the temple before the gathered people and officials.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.36.28	The burned words are rewritten	The commentary says the teaching endured from the first pages to its present recitation; after Jehoiakim burns the scroll, Jeremiah is told to write the same words again, showing the message surviving destruction of its copy.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hab.2.2	A vision made readable	The commentary pictures old writing as an open, legible surface; Habakkuk is told to write the vision plainly on tablets so a reader can run with it, explicitly joining a written revelation to its public transmission.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.6.6	Words kept in the heart	The commentary says the pages' message reaches the Prophet as recitation and is retained; Moses commands Israel to keep these words in the heart, joining scripture with inward memory.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.6.7	Words recited to children	The commentary treats the old teaching as a living word heard by later people; Deuteronomy requires parents to teach and speak it at home, on the road, at bedtime, and at rising.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.78.3	What fathers heard is told onward	The commentary answers the claim that the message is new by locating it among earlier generations; the psalm says its teaching was heard and known from the fathers who told it.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.78.4	The next generation is not left ignorant	The commentary says an ancient warning remains present rather than forgotten; the psalm refuses to hide the fathers' praise-worthy acts from their children and pledges to tell the next generation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.78.7	Remembering leads to trust and obedience	The commentary links recited remembrance to fear of God and the surah's counsel; Psalm 78 says the next generation should hope in God, not forget his works, and keep his commands.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.7	Ask the elders about days of old	The commentary answers “we never heard this from our ancestors” by asserting ancient continuity; Moses tells the audience to remember former days and ask their fathers and elders.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.30.14	The word is near, in mouth and heart	The commentary says the Prophet receives the pages' content by recitation rather than by handling them; Deuteronomy describes the commandment as near, in the hearer's mouth and heart, ready to be done.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.8	God's word outlasts fading life	The commentary says the world passes but the statement about the lasting hereafter has itself endured; Isaiah contrasts withering grass and flowers with God's word standing forever.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.119.89	The word fixed forever	The commentary treats the first pages as a durable witness across generations; the psalm says God's word is established in heaven forever, supplying a concrete scriptural image of permanence.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.16	A book of remembrance for the God-fearing	The commentary connects fear of God, remembrance, and preserved pages; Malachi describes those who fear the LORD speaking together while a book of remembrance is written before him for them.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.12.4	Prophetic words sealed for the end	The commentary says the first writing bears witness to the final outcome; Daniel is told to shut up and seal the words until the time of the end, a different but concrete model of an ancient text preserved for a later age.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.16	Each person answers for their own sin	The commentary joins self-purification to the saying that no bearer carries another's burden; Deuteronomy's legal rule says parent and child are not executed for one another's sin, but each for their own.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.18.20	A child does not bear a parent's iniquity	The commentary reads purification as one's own act and cites the rule that none bears another's load; Ezekiel explicitly assigns guilt to the person who sins, not to that person's father or son.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.18.21	Turning from sin brings life	The commentary's “one who purifies himself” is an individual turning toward good; Ezekiel says the person who turns from transgression, keeps the statutes, and does right shall live.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.31.30	Each dies for their own iniquity	The commentary's cited page teaching denies transferred burdens; Jeremiah answers the sour-grapes proverb by saying each person dies for their own iniquity, sharpening the move from inherited blame to individual responsibility.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.13	Fear God and keep the commandments	The commentary's nearby verses join fearing God, purification, and prayer to the choice of the hereafter; Ecclesiastes closes by making fear of God and keeping his commandments the whole human duty.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.14	Every deed comes to judgment	The commentary places the more enduring hereafter against present preference; Ecclesiastes grounds that contrast in God's judgment of every deed, including what is hidden.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.12.2	Awakening to everlasting life	The commentary says the hereafter is better and more enduring than present life; Daniel's sleepers awake, some to everlasting life and others to disgrace, giving that future a resurrection setting.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.49.17	Wealth cannot follow at death	The commentary challenges preferring the near life to the lasting one; Psalm 49 says a person takes nothing from wealth at death and that splendor does not descend after him.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	Wisdom of Solomon 2:6	The wicked choose immediate pleasure	The commentary rejects preferring the present life because the hereafter is more enduring; Wisdom 2 puts the opposite case in the mouths of the wicked, who urge one another to enjoy present goods and youth.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	Wisdom of Solomon 3:1	The righteous are safe beyond apparent death	The commentary says the afterlife is the better, abiding outcome; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God's hand and seem only to have died, directly overturning a worldly judgment of their fate.
strong	tevrat	paralel	2 Maccabees 7:9	A martyr chooses resurrection over survival	The commentary says the later life is better than the near one; the second brother accepts death under torture while confessing that the King of the world will raise the faithful to renewed life.
strong	tevrat	paralel	2 Maccabees 7:14	Hope beyond death	The commentary makes the enduring hereafter the reason not to privilege present life; the fourth brother says he hopes to be raised by God, while his persecutor has no share in resurrection to life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1John.2.17	The world passes; God's will remains	The commentary contrasts the passing world with what is more enduring; John says the world and its desire are passing away, while the one who does God's will remains forever.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.11.26	Moses values the future reward above Egypt	The commentary names Moses' pages as a source for rejecting worldly preference; Hebrews depicts Moses refusing Egypt's treasures and choosing reproach because he was looking to the reward.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.8.36	The whole world cannot outweigh life	The commentary asks why one would prefer the near world over the lasting hereafter; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.20	Treasure that does not decay	The commentary calls the hereafter more enduring than worldly life; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy it.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.18	Visible things are temporary	The commentary says the world passes while the message about the hereafter lasts; Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.15.4	Earlier writings teach and sustain hope	The commentary says 87:18 answers novelty by locating its teaching in first pages; Paul says what was written in former times was written for present instruction and endurance, to give hope.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.10.11	Ancient events written for later admonition	The commentary treats old pages as a warning to present hearers who prefer the world; Paul says the earlier events occurred as examples and were written down for admonition of later generations.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Gal.3.8	Scripture preached beforehand to Abraham	The commentary names Abraham among the recipients of the first pages; Paul reads Genesis as scripture foreseeing the Gentiles' justification and announcing the gospel beforehand to Abraham.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:John.5.46	Moses' writing witnesses to a later message	The commentary answers that the present teaching is not a new invention by naming Moses' pages; Jesus says Moses wrote about him, making the older Torah a witness to a later proclamation and criticizing hearers who reject both.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.26.22	Paul claims continuity with Moses and the prophets	The commentary's central claim is that the current warning was already in ancient pages; Paul tells Agrippa that he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets said would happen.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.3.15	Scripture known from childhood guides salvation	The commentary describes an old text whose recited teaching still instructs its hearers; Timothy's sacred writings, known from childhood, are said to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.24	Flesh fades like grass	The commentary's adjacent claim is that worldly life passes while its message endures; Peter compares all flesh to grass and its glory to a flower that falls.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.25	The preached word endures	The commentary says the ancient pages' statement has survived to the Prophet's recitation; Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the gospel preached to his readers.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	The dead judged from opened books	The commentary links pages, deeds, and the eventual outcome; Revelation depicts books opened at judgment and the dead judged according to what was written in them and what they had done.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.5	Each carries their own load	The commentary's reading of purification is personal and is paired with “no bearer bears another's burden”; Paul says each person will carry their own load.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.14.12	Each gives an account to God	The commentary connects the old pages' warning with each person's own conduct; Paul says each of us will give an account of himself to God.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.5.10	Each receives for deeds done in the body	The commentary links personal purification and the enduring hereafter; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat so each may receive for what was done in the body.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.6	God repays according to deeds	The commentary pairs individual action with the coming outcome; Paul says God will repay each person according to their deeds, explicitly connecting conduct and judgment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.7	Eternal life for those seeking what lasts	The commentary says the afterlife is better and more enduring; Paul specifies eternal life for those who persevere in good work while seeking glory, honor, and immortality.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1John.3.3	Hope purifies the hopeful person	The commentary says the successful person “purifies himself”; John uses the same reflexive moral pattern, saying everyone with this hope purifies himself as Christ is pure.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.4.8	Clean hands and purified hearts	The commentary joins purification to remembrance of God and prayer; James calls those drawing near to God to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.1.15	Prayer with unclean hands is rejected	The commentary places purification beside remembering God's name and prayer; Isaiah depicts worshippers spreading hands in prayer, but God refuses to hear because their hands are full of blood.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.1.16	Wash and make yourselves clean	The commentary says the person who purifies himself succeeds; Isaiah's answer to corrupt worship is a concrete command to wash and cleanse, then cease doing evil.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.1.17	Purity expressed as justice	The commentary links purification and prayer, not mere ritual display; Isaiah specifies learning good, seeking justice, and defending the vulnerable as the ethical turn that follows cleansing.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.14	God brings grass up for cattle	The commentary links the surah's opening pasture to Moses' description of God sending rain and bringing out plants; the psalm says God makes grass grow for livestock and plants for human use.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.16.29	Moses and the prophets already speak	The commentary says people asking for new sheets lack fear, since the old pages already give warning; in Jesus' story Abraham answers a dead rich man's request by pointing to Moses and the prophets, which his brothers should hear.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.16.31	A new sign cannot replace hearing scripture	The commentary says another page would not cure refusal to heed the existing warning; Abraham's reply is that those who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by someone rising from the dead.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.10.12	Fear, love, and service	The commentary joins fear of God to purification and prayer; Moses asks Israel to fear the LORD, walk in his ways, love and serve him with all the heart and soul.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.30.6	God purifies the heart	The commentary describes a person purifying himself, while Ezekiel and other texts personalize responsibility; Deuteronomy adds that God circumcises the heart so Israel may love him, making divine aid part of inner renewal.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.30.19	Choose life rather than death	The commentary says hearers prefer the near life despite the better hereafter; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life by loving and clinging to God.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.2	The righteous meditate on Torah continually	The commentary says the old word is recited, remembered, and acted on; Psalm 1 locates the righteous person's delight in the LORD's instruction, meditated on day and night.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.6	Two paths end differently	The commentary's world/hereafter contrast culminates in different outcomes; Psalm 1 says the LORD knows the way of the righteous while the way of the wicked perishes.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.49.16	Do not envy worldly splendor	The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life; Psalm 49 tells the hearer not to fear when another grows rich and his household's glory increases, setting up the death-boundary made explicit in v.17.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.24.12	God weighs the heart and repays deeds	The commentary says each person's choice matters and cites the rule that no one bears another's burden; Proverbs answers the excuse “we did not know” by saying the heart-weigher sees and repays each according to work.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.18.30	Turn and live	The commentary's purification is a person's own turning, not a transferred act; Ezekiel calls the house of Israel to repent and turn from transgressions so iniquity will not be a stumbling block.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.7	Remember the ancestral teaching	The commentary answers a claim of novelty by invoking what came from the first ancestors; Moses directs hearers to consult fathers and elders about the former days.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.22	Remember Moses' Torah before the coming day	The commentary names Moses' pages and says their teaching addresses the final outcome; Malachi closes by telling Israel to remember the Torah commanded to Moses at Horeb before the coming day of the LORD.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.46.10	The end announced from the beginning	The commentary says the first pages already tell where all things will end; Isaiah portrays God as declaring the end from the beginning and bringing his purpose to completion.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Josh.1.8	Moses' book leads the successor	The commentary pictures the first writings as going ahead and later speech following their path; Joshua, Moses' successor, is told to keep the Torah book in his mouth, meditate on it, and act according to it.
medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.26.5	Abraham obeys God's commandments	The commentary names Abraham as recipient of ancient pages; Genesis says Abraham obeyed God's voice and kept his charge, commandments, statutes, and instructions, giving a concrete ancestral precedent for the teaching.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.15.6	Abraham's faith counted as righteousness	The commentary names Abraham among the first recipients; Genesis presents Abraham believing God and being counted righteous, the verse Paul later treats as an early scriptural witness to faith.
medium	tevrat	motif	Sirach 44:20	Abraham keeps the law and covenant	The commentary's final verse names Abraham and Moses together; Ben Sira remembers Abraham as keeping the law of the Most High and entering a covenant, showing a Jewish retelling that makes him a model of ancient fidelity.
medium	tevrat	motif	Sirach 45:1	Moses' memory is praised	The commentary names Moses as bearer of the old pages; Ben Sira's praise of the ancestors turns to Moses as beloved by God and honored, adding a Jewish wisdom portrait of the named lawgiver.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Genesis Rabbah 64:4	Abraham observed Torah before Sinai	The commentary's “first pages” include Abraham as well as Moses; this midrash reads Genesis 26:5 to say Abraham kept the Torah before it was given, extending the antiquity of revealed practice to the patriarch.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Targum Onqelos on Genesis 26:5	Abraham's obedience rendered as Torah observance	The commentary names Abraham's pages but leaves their contents open; Onqelos renders the Genesis account in terms of Abraham keeping God's commandments and teachings, giving an Aramaic interpretive bridge from the patriarch to Torah.
medium	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 3:16	A ledger records every deed	The commentary connects enduring pages with personal accountability; Avot pictures an open book and a recording hand alongside judgment, making written record a rabbinic image for the moral accounting implied by the pages.
medium	tevrat	motif	1 Enoch 81:1	Heavenly tablets record human deeds	The commentary says a divine book preserves what happened to the first generations; Enoch is shown heavenly tablets and reads what is written there, an apocalyptic expansion of memory and record beyond earthly pages.
medium	tevrat	motif	1 Enoch 47:3	The righteous are remembered in books	The commentary links fearers and a preserved record; Enoch depicts the books of the righteous and their prayers brought before the Lord of Spirits, a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to a heavenly book of remembrance.
medium	tevrat	motif	Josephus, Against Apion 1.38	A bounded ancient scriptural collection	The commentary answers that the message is not a new invention by locating it in first pages; Josephus defends the antiquity and counted extent of Jewish sacred books, showing how a Jewish author argued for a stable inherited corpus.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	Augustine, City of God 10.32	Christian religion claimed as ancient	The commentary answers novelty by saying the teaching was present in the first pages; Augustine argues that what is now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients from the beginning, a patristic reading of present faith as recovery rather than late invention.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.119.9	Purity by guarding the word	The commentary joins self-purification to the recited old teaching; Psalm 119 asks how a young person's way can be kept pure and answers by guarding it according to God's word.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.119.11	The word stored in the heart	The commentary says revelation reaches the Prophet by recitation and is not forgotten; the psalmist stores God's word in the heart to avoid sin, linking remembered scripture with moral purification.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.24.4	Clean hands and a pure heart in worship	The commentary joins purification to prayer; the psalm describes the one who may ascend God's holy place as having clean hands and a pure heart, tying inward and outward purity to worship.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.51.12	A prayer for a clean heart	The commentary describes the person who purifies himself; David asks God to create a clean heart in him, adding a distinct emphasis on purification received from God rather than self-congratulation.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Kgs.22.8	A lost Torah scroll is rediscovered	The commentary says first-page teaching endured into the present; in Kings, Hilkiah finds a Torah book in the temple after it had been absent from the king's practice, and its recovery prompts reform, complicating any simple picture of uninterrupted access.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.36.23	A king burns the scroll	The commentary says the old word has lasted; Jeremiah's scroll is cut and burned by Jehoiakim, a concrete counter-image of the vulnerability of the physical page before the message is rewritten in v.28.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Wisd.3.4	The righteous' hope is full of immortality	The commentary calls the hereafter more enduring than this life; Wisdom says the righteous may seem punished at death, yet their hope is full of immortality, correcting the worldly reading of their fate.
medium	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 3:9	Those who trust God abide with him	The commentary calls the later life more enduring; Wisdom says those who trust God will understand truth and abide with him in love, specifying the lasting communion behind its reversal of worldly judgment.
medium	tevrat	motif	Tobit 12:8	Prayer, fasting, and almsgiving together	The commentary pairs purification and prayer and its refs mention prayer with almsgiving; Tobit says prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving, giving a Jewish ethical-worship combination rather than treating prayer as an isolated rite.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.19	Treasure laid up for the future life	The commentary contrasts present worldly preference with the lasting hereafter; Paul tells the rich to store up treasure as a foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.21	Riches gathered only for oneself do not last	The commentary warns against preferring the near life; Jesus' rich fool stores goods for himself but dies that night, and the story calls him poor toward God.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.11.16	The patriarchs seek a better country	The commentary names Abraham among the first pages and says the hereafter is better; Hebrews reads the patriarchs as desiring a better, heavenly country and a city prepared by God.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.1.2	The gospel promised beforehand in scripture	The commentary's claim is that the present word is already in the earliest writings; Paul introduces the gospel as promised beforehand through God's prophets in holy scriptures.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Luke.24.27	Moses and the prophets interpreted as witnesses	The commentary says the recent teaching is contained in earlier pages; Luke depicts Jesus interpreting what the scriptures say about him, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, a Christian rereading of the old texts as testimony to the present.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.4.21	A written prophecy declared fulfilled in hearing	The commentary joins pages to a word heard in the present; after reading Isaiah in the synagogue, Jesus says the scripture has been fulfilled in the hearers' hearing.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.10	Earlier prophets searched the promised grace	The commentary says the first pages already contain the later warning; Peter describes prophets who searched and inquired about the grace now announced, connecting prior revelation with a later proclamation.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.12	Earlier prophets served later hearers	The commentary says the old word has reached the Prophet's audience; Peter says the prophets were serving not themselves but later readers, to whom the gospel is now announced.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.3.2	A letter read in human hearts	The commentary says the pages' content can be present without a page in the Prophet's hand; Paul calls the Corinthians a letter known and read by all, a human community serving as written testimony.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.3.3	Writing by the Spirit on hearts	The commentary contrasts a physical page with a message recited and retained; Paul says the Spirit writes on tablets of human hearts rather than stone, developing a Christian image of inwardly carried scripture.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.1.1	God spoke formerly through prophets	The commentary says the same enduring warning was present in older pages; Hebrews describes God speaking to ancestors through prophets in many times and ways, then frames the present as a further stage of that speech.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.7.1	Self-cleansing perfected in fear of God	The commentary joins purification with fear and prayer; Paul urges believers to cleanse themselves from defilement and perfect holiness in fear of God, an explicit ethical counterpart to the surah's purifier who fears.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.18.14	The repentant prayer is accepted over self-display	The commentary warns that self-purification is not self-praise; Jesus' parable ends with the tax collector, not the self-congratulating Pharisee, going home justified, clarifying the difference between turning toward God and claiming one's own merit.
medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.7.11	Moses' signs and Pharaoh's magicians	The commentary cites opponents of Moses calling his clear signs fabricated magic and unheard by their ancestors; Exodus stages a Moses-and-Pharaoh sign contest in which Pharaoh's magicians answer with their arts, a related scene framed as rival performance rather than ancestral novelty.
weak	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Kgs.22.10	The recovered book is read to the king	The commentary presents the ancient pages as a witness to the present; the king's secretary reads the rediscovered Torah book to Josiah, but the episode concerns recovery after neglect, so the link is about renewed hearing rather than uninterrupted preservation.
EOF
